extracted.intended_audience: students, thinkers, and designers of representative constitutions; legislators and informed citizens
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and practical principles for structuring representative institutions (remuneration, term length, pledges, bicameralism), aimed at balancing popular control with the benefits of superior ability and minority representation. Focuses on what institutional features promote responsible, capable, and restrained government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remuneration of members of Parliament (indemnity not salary)
rubrics_metrics.description: If payment is necessary, it should be an indemnity for loss of time or money, not a salary; a salary would make the office a profession pursued for pecuniary returns and attract adventurers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A salary would convert the occupation into a pursuit for pecuniary return, encouraging demoralizing competition and pandering to electors. Public subscription to support an otherwise impecunious but qualified representative is unobjectionable (as with Andrew Marvell). The indemnity model preserves independence and limits attraction of those primarily seeking pay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making parliamentary office a salaried profession
rubrics_metrics.description: No remuneration should be set at a level that would attract persons seriously engaged in other lucrative professions or make the post chiefly pursued for its pecuniary returns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High fixed salaries would encourage 'adventurers of a low class' and produce an 'auction' of promises to electors; remuneration should not transform representation into a career that fosters flatterers and courtly vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term length balance (duration of Parliaments)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term should balance keeping representatives accountable (not so long they forget responsibility) and giving them enough time to be judged by a course of action rather than a single act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where democratic power is weak or representatives enter aristocratic atmospheres, frequent returns (even three years may be nearly too long) are necessary. Where democracy is ascendant and publicity/the press keep representatives constantly judged, less than five years would hardly be sufficient. Seven years is unnecessarily long but tolerable given the possibility of early dissolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of renewal: general elections vs. staggered renewal
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer general renewal of the whole House at the end of terms rather than individual members vacating on different schedules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General elections allow prompt removal of a majority offensive to the nation and provide a periodic 'muster' to gauge national opinion. Partial or gradual renewal risks an indefinite divergence between assembly and constituency and fails to conclusively ascertain relative party strengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of executive dissolution in term design
rubrics_metrics.description: The possibility of earlier dissolution by the executive affects the practical incentives and makes longer formal terms less problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if formal terms are long (e.g., seven years), the looming possibility of dissolution keeps members mindful of constituents; the executive's dissolution power interacts with term length to shape representative behavior (to be treated alongside executive constitution/function).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pledges and instructions: representatives should not be strictly bound
rubrics_metrics.description: A legislator ought generally to vote according to his own judgment rather than being mechanically bound to constituents' instructions; the delegation theory is false in principle and harmful in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While electors can by choice reduce a representative to a delegate, constitutional morality and the value of superior wisdom imply that absolute conformity should not be required. Representatives should have unfettered discretion except in special circumstances where the electorate's choice is severely constrained.

rubrics_metrics.name: When pledges may be justified (exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actual pledges may be required only when electors are so narrowed in choice by social or family circumstances that they must fix on persons presumptively under hostile partialities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If constituencies are forced to choose among persons of a station or class different from their own and with conflicting class interests, they are justified in exacting pledges on key measures as safeguards of their interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electors' entitlement to knowledge of candidate opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Electors are entitled to a full knowledge of the political opinions and sentiments of candidates and may justly reject candidates who differ on foundational articles of political belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Candidates should disclose their expected guiding opinions; electors should weigh these disclosures and may overlook non-fundamental differences in favor of superior ability, but must be able to reject candidates on vital convictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of superior mental ability in representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: It is important to secure representatives possessing superior intellect, study, and practical discipline even if their opinions sometimes differ from the majority of electors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electors who value superior wisdom should be willing to tolerate differences on non-fundamental matters and actively seek representatives of high calibre; institutions should encourage deference to proven ability for the public good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical criteria for assessing a candidate's ability
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary electors should rely on identifiable signs of wisdom and competence when choosing representatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful tests include prior public services, performance in significant posts, authorship and practical success of measures, predictions verified by events, advice that produced good consequences, reputation among disinterested experts, and recommendations from respected authorities; for untried candidates, reputation and endorsements are key.

rubrics_metrics.name: When electors should dismiss a representative
rubrics_metrics.description: Electors may properly dismiss a representative if he intends to govern in opposition to the people's fundamental convictions; changes of opinion honestly avowed should not automatically cause dismissal unless they touch vital points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences not related to fundamentals should be tolerated for the greater benefit of ability; but when issues central to a people's political life are at stake, the representative's contrary position justifies rejection at the next opportunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Against pure delegation under universal suffrage
rubrics_metrics.description: If the constitution lacks provisions for representation of minorities or differentiation of voting power (e.g., according to education), leaving representatives unfettered is especially important; otherwise delegation leads to exclusive majority rule and class legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a system where minorities have no constitutional voice, requiring delegates would permit the majority (especially uneducated operative classes) to enforce class legislation; unfettered discretion for representatives may be the only means to allow minority or educated opinions to reach legislature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and limits of a Second Chamber (bicameralism)
rubrics_metrics.description: A second chamber can be useful but its value depends on composition and social support; two chambers of similar composition add limited additional check, while dissimilar composition may act as a restraint on democracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two similarly composed houses mainly cause delay and occasional appeals to electors with roughly balanced costs/benefits. The chief benefit of bicameralism is psychological and institutional: preventing any set of persons from consulting only themselves and encouraging conciliation and compromise. An aristocratic second chamber is effective only where aristocratic social support exists; in a truly democratic society it would be ineffectual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-offs of having two chambers
rubrics_metrics.description: Two chambers may impede measures by requiring consent of both, but they also check precipitancy and teach conciliation; the delay can be offset by benefits of mutual give-and-take.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inconvenience of delay might be balanced by the advantage of appealing to electors or allowing further deliberation; the mutual necessity to consider another authority reduces the corrupting influence of undivided power.
